content: Tartaric acid is a white, crystalline organic acid that naturally occurs in various plants, including grapes, bananas, and tamarinds. It is one of the primary acids found in wine and is often added to other foods to impart a sour taste. Additionally, it serves as an antioxidant. The salts derived from tartaric acid are referred to as tartrates. Chemically, tartaric acid is a dihydroxy derivative of dicarboxylic acid. Historically, it was first isolated from potassium tartrate (known as tartar) around 800 AD by the Persian alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan, who also contributed to many foundational chemical processes still in use today. The modern method of isolating tartaric acid was developed in 1769 by the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele. In 1832, Jean Baptiste Biot discovered the chirality of tartaric acid by observing its ability to rotate polarized light. Louis Pasteur furthered this research in 1847 by studying the asymmetric shapes of tartaric acid crystals and was the first to isolate a pure sample of levotartaric acid. Naturally occurring tartaric acid is chiral, meaning its molecules are non-superimposable mirror images. This property makes it a valuable raw material in organic chemistry for synthesizing other chiral molecules. The naturally occurring form is L-(+)-tartaric acid, also known as dextrotartaric acid. Its enantiomer, D-(−)-tartaric acid or levotartaric acid, and the achiral form, mesotartaric acid, can be synthesized artificially. It is important to note that the prefixes dextro and levo refer to the direction of optical rotation, not the D/L configuration derived from glyceraldehyde. Levotartaric and dextrotartaric acids are enantiomers, while mesotartaric acid is a diastereomer of both. A racemic mixture, DL-tartaric acid, is a 1:1 combination of the levo and dextro forms and is optically inactive. This racemic acid was historically called racemic acid, derived from the Latin word racemus, meaning a bunch of grapes. Over time, the term racemic has come to describe any 1:1 enantiomeric mixture, known as a racemate. Tartaric acid has several important derivatives, including its salts. Potassium bitartrate, commonly known as cream of tartar, is one such derivative. Another is potassium sodium tartrate, also called Rochelle salt, which is used as a mild laxative. Antimony potassium tartrate, or tartar emetic, is another derivative. Tartaric acid acts as a muscle toxin by inhibiting the production of malic acid, and in high doses, it can cause paralysis and death. The minimum recorded fatal dose for humans is approximately 7.5 grams per kilogram of body weight. Despite its toxicity at high doses, tartaric acid is widely used in food, particularly in sour-tasting sweets. As a food additive, it functions as an antioxidant and is labeled with the E number E334. Tartrates are also used as antioxidants or emulsifiers. When cream of tartar is mixed with water, it forms a suspension that effectively cleans copper coins by dissolving the copper(II) oxide layer on their surface. The resulting copper(II)-tartrate complex is highly water-soluble. In the context of wine, tartaric acid is recognizable to wine drinkers as the source of wine diamonds, which are small potassium bitartrate crystals that sometimes form on the cork. These crystals, though harmless, are occasionally mistaken for broken glass. Many winemakers prevent their formation through a process called cold stabilization. Historically, the tartrates that accumulated inside aging barrels were a significant industrial source of potassium bitartrate. Chemically, tartaric acid plays a crucial role in winemaking by lowering the pH of fermenting grape must to a level that inhibits the growth of spoilage bacteria. It also acts as a preservative after fermentation. In terms of taste, tartaric acid contributes to the tartness of wine, although citric and malic acids also play a role. Modern winemaking practices, such as extended hang time (allowing grapes to remain on the vine until they nearly become raisins), can significantly reduce the tartaric acid content in wine. This results in a smoother wine but may make it less compatible with food pairings.
